description:
## Why

Every workload ticket teaches us something about performance on the BEAM: which Elixir spellings the JIT makes fast, where the cliffs are, how scheduling and the NIF boundary behave, and what makes a defk kernel vectorise or not. Today those findings are scattered: the 'what was tried' tables in about 25 example headers, examples/README.md 'Measuring correctly', docs/beam-nifs.md, docs/research/*, README known limitations, and ticket comments. Nobody can find them again, and a future us (or a new contributor) will re-measure what we already know or repeat a mistake we already made.

## What

docs/performance.md (name open), a living guide written for maintainers first and users second. Each finding is one short entry:

- the claim, in one sentence (what to do or avoid);
- the numbers, and the conditions they hold under (machine, OTP/Elixir version, size, load: provisional or quiet);
- a small code sketch of the fast and the slow spelling;
- the source (example file, ticket, commit) so it can be re-checked;
- status: measured, provisional, or superseded (with what replaced it).

Suggested sections (adjust to what the harvest finds):
1. Measuring honestly: the rules from examples/README.md, why best-of and GC, tick gaps, why load makes numbers provisional, comparing like with like (parallel vs parallel, one process vs one call).
2. Fast Elixir on binaries and numbers: binary append optimised in place vs iodata vs lists; binary matching and comprehensions into <<>>; float boxing in lists; small integers vs bignums (the ~60-bit cliff: split 64-bit work into 32-bit halves, as geohash_crc and gorilla did); 32-bit words beating 64-bit words on the JIT (ws_masking); :crypto.exor with a doubled key; batching several items per recursion step (rolling_stats).
3. BIFs and OTP libraries that are already native: :binary.match, :erlang.crc32, String.valid?, :crypto, :zlib, and their throughput, so nobody writes a kernel to beat them.
4. Parallelism: Task.async_stream vs Task.async + await_many for short kernel tasks, scheduler wake-up and the reductions a kernel charges, chunk sizes that spread, +swt very_low (defk-8qs, defk-6lr).
5. The NIF boundary: per-call cost (~0.1-0.2 us), packing lists costs more than the work (poor_list_data), batch size break-even (geohash single point), sub-binaries and copies.
6. Making a defk kernel fast: strips and safepoints, flagged checks and replay (defk-6tt, defk-hki), what blocks vectorisation (in-order float reductions, per-operation checks, defk-agp), facts that drop bounds checks, reading use Defk, report: :full.
7. When a hand-written or wrapper NIF is still the answer, and dirty vs yielding.
8. Open questions and myths we've disproved.

## How it stays alive

- Harvest: go through every examples/*.exs header and examples/README.md row, docs/beam-nifs.md, the research docs and closed workload tickets' comments; turn each finding into an entry with its source. Don't re-measure in this ticket; mark what came from loaded runs as provisional.
- Process: add a step to examples/README.md 'Adding an example' and to the workload evidence bar (the template text the defk-9p6 / defk-52v tickets quote): 'add or update the guide entries for what you learned (including what didn't help)'. Propose the matching line for AGENTS.md (a project rule change: confirm with the maintainer before committing it).
- When the quiet-machine snapshot (defk-sgw.4) lands, update the provisional entries it covers. When OTP or Elixir changes version, entries are tied to their version so they can be re-checked.
- It becomes a HexDocs extra once the docs setup exists (defk-djy.1); the Measuring guide (defk-djy.4) links to it instead of repeating it.

Done when the harvest covers every example and the sources above, each entry has numbers, conditions and a source, the 'Adding an example' step and evidence-bar text are updated, and the guide is linked from README and examples/README.md.
title: Living guide: what is fast on the BEAM, what isn't, and how to fix it (for future us)
